arguments.title: Results
arguments.content:
### 3.1 Study Selection and Characteristics

The initial search across PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar yielded 4,867 records. After removing 1,942 duplicates, 2,925 records were screened by title and abstract, of which 2,637 were excluded as they did not meet the inclusion criteria. The remaining 288 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility, and 176 were excluded due to incomplete data (n=68), study design not meeting inclusion criteria (n=52), population outside target age range (n=31), and duplicate publications (n=25). A total of 112 studies met all eligibility criteria and were included in the systematic review, of which 58 were included in the quantitative meta-analysis. The PRISMA 2020 flow diagram illustrating this process is presented in Figure 1.

The 112 included studies comprised 89 cross-sectional studies, 18 cohort studies, and 5 case-control studies. The total sample size across all studies was 1,247,839 children under five years of age. Studies were published between 2010 and 2024, with the majority (68.8%) published after 2018. All studies were conducted in Indonesia, covering 31 of 34 provinces. The quality assessment using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale and its adapted version for cross-sectional studies revealed that 78 studies (69.6%) were of high quality, 28 (25.0%) of moderate quality, and 6 (5.4%) of low quality.

### 3.2 Geographic Distribution of Studies

The geographic distribution of included studies showed a concentration in Java Island, particularly in East Java (n=19, 17.0%), Central Java (n=15, 13.4%), and West Java (n=14, 12.5%). Sumatra contributed 24 studies (21.4%), with the highest numbers from North Sumatra (n=8) and Aceh (n=6). Studies from Sulawesi (n=11, 9.8%), Kalimantan (n=8, 7.1%), and the eastern regions including Nusa Tenggara, Maluku, and Papua (n=12, 10.7%) were comparatively underrepresented. Urban-based studies accounted for 58% (n=65), while rural-based studies comprised 42% (n=47).

### 3.3 Pooled Prevalence of Stunting

The pooled prevalence of stunting among children under five in Indonesia, based on 112 studies with random-effects meta-analysis, was 31.8% (95% CI: 29.4%–34.3%), with substantial heterogeneity (I² = 97.2%, p < 0.001). Subgroup analysis by time period revealed a declining trend: studies from 2010–2014 reported a pooled prevalence of 37.2% (95% CI: 33.1%–41.4%), those from 2015–2019 reported 32.5% (95% CI: 29.8%–35.3%), and those from 2020–2024 reported 27.9% (95% CI: 24.6%–31.4%). The decline was statistically significant (p for trend < 0.001). Subgroup analysis by island region showed the highest prevalence in East Nusa Tenggara (42.7%; 95% CI: 37.2%–48.3%), followed by Papua (40.1%; 95% CI: 34.5%–46.0%), and the lowest in Bali (21.4%; 95% CI: 17.8%–25.5%).

### 3.4 Maternal Determinants of Stunting

Maternal factors were consistently associated with stunting risk. Maternal height < 150 cm was significantly associated with child stunting (pooled OR = 2.31; 95% CI: 1.92–2.78; I² = 68.4%; n = 34 studies). Maternal education below senior high school level was also a significant risk factor (pooled OR = 1.87; 95% CI: 1.64–2.13; I² = 72.1%; n = 47 studies). Inadequate antenatal care visits (< 4 visits) showed a significant association (pooled OR = 1.56; 95% CI: 1.34–1.82; I² = 58.3%; n = 28 studies). Maternal anemia during pregnancy was associated with an increased risk of stunting (pooled OR = 1.73; 95% CI: 1.41–2.12; I² = 63.7%; n = 19 studies). Short birth spacing (< 24 months) was also a significant risk factor (pooled OR = 1.64; 95% CI: 1.38–1.95; I² = 55.2%; n = 22 studies).

### 3.5 Child-Specific Determinants of Stunting

Low birth weight (< 2,500 g) was the strongest child-specific predictor of stunting (pooled OR = 2.97; 95% CI: 2.54–3.48; I² = 71.8%; n = 52 studies). Male sex was modestly but significantly associated with stunting (pooled OR = 1.21; 95% CI: 1.12–1.31; I² = 45.3%; n = 61 studies). Incomplete or nonexclusive breastfeeding for the first six months was a significant risk factor (pooled OR = 1.68; 95% CI: 1.47–1.92; I² = 62.9%; n = 38 studies). Inadequate complementary feeding practices (minimum dietary diversity not met) was significantly associated with stunting (pooled OR = 1.82; 95% CI: 1.55–2.14; I² = 67.4%; n = 31 studies). Recurrent infections, particularly diarrheal episodes (≥3 in six months), increased stunting risk (pooled OR = 1.94; 95% CI: 1.61–2.34; I² = 58.6%; n = 24 studies).

### 3.6 Socioeconomic and Environmental Determinants

Low household income (lowest vs. highest quintile) was significantly associated with stunting (pooled OR = 2.14; 95% CI: 1.85–2.48; I² = 74.2%; n = 41 studies). Rural residence was associated with increased stunting risk (pooled OR = 1.48; 95% CI: 1.32–1.66; I² = 63.5%; n = 38 studies). Inadequate access to improved sanitation facilities was a significant environmental risk factor (pooled OR = 1.71; 95% CI: 1.49–1.96; I² = 59.8%; n = 29 studies). Unimproved drinking water sources were also associated with stunting (pooled OR = 1.43; 95% CI: 1.25–1.64; I² = 52.1%; n = 26 studies). Household food insecurity was a significant predictor (pooled OR = 1.89; 95% CI: 1.58–2.26; I² = 66.3%; n = 18 studies).

### 3.7 Meta-Regression and Sensitivity Analysis

Meta-regression analysis identified several significant moderators of the stunting prevalence estimates. Study design (cross-sectional vs. cohort, p = 0.038), sampling method (probability vs. non-probability, p = 0.012), and geographic region (p = 0.004) significantly contributed to heterogeneity. Year of publication was inversely associated with stunting prevalence (β = -0.018; p = 0.003), confirming the temporal declining trend. Sensitivity analysis using leave-one-out methods confirmed the robustness of the pooled estimates, with no single study substantially altering the overall pooled prevalence by more than 0.8 percentage points.

### 3.8 Publication Bias Assessment

Visual inspection of funnel plots for the primary outcome (stunting prevalence) suggested asymmetry. Egger's regression test confirmed significant publication bias (intercept = 1.82; 95% CI: 0.74–2.90; p = 0.001). The trim-and-fill method imputed 14 missing studies, and the adjusted pooled prevalence was 29.3% (95% CI: 26.5%–32.2%), suggesting that the unadjusted estimate may be slightly inflated. For determinant analyses, publication bias was assessed for each risk factor, with significant asymmetry detected for maternal education and low birth weight analyses, though adjusted estimates remained statistically significant.

arguments.title: Discussion
arguments.content:
### 4.1 Summary of Key Findings

This systematic review and meta-analysis, encompassing 112 studies and over 1.2 million children under five across Indonesia, estimated a pooled stunting prevalence of 31.8% (95% CI: 29.4%–34.3%). Although this represents a significant decline from earlier periods (37.2% before 2014 to 27.9% in 2020–2024), the prevalence remains substantially above the World Health Assembly target of 14% by 2025 and the Sustainable Development Goal target of ending all forms of malnutrition by 2030. The analysis identified a constellation of maternal, child-specific, socioeconomic, and environmental determinants that interact synergistically to drive stunting in Indonesia.

### 4.2 Interpretation of Prevalence Trends

The declining trend in stunting prevalence observed in this meta-analysis is consistent with national surveillance data from the Indonesian Ministry of Health (Riskesdas and SSGI surveys), which documented a reduction from 37.2% in 2013 to 21.6% in 2022. However, the pooled estimate from this review (31.8%) is higher than the most recent national estimate, likely reflecting the inclusion of subnational studies from high-burden regions such as East Nusa Tenggara and Papua, where prevalence rates exceed 40%. This discrepancy underscores the importance of examining geographic heterogeneity when evaluating national progress. The substantial between-study heterogeneity (I² = 97.2%) reflects genuine variation in stunting prevalence across regions, time periods, and populations, which was partially explained by meta-regression.

### 4.3 Maternal Determinants in the Indonesian Context

The association between short maternal stature (<150 cm) and child stunting (OR = 2.31) reflects an intergenerational cycle of malnutrition that has been well-documented in low- and middle-income countries. However, in the Indonesian context, this relationship may be partly mediated by socioeconomic factors that affect both maternal and child nutrition across generations. The significance of maternal education (OR = 1.87) highlights the role of health literacy and caregiving practices in child nutrition. Notably, the association between inadequate antenatal care and stunting (OR = 1.56) points to missed opportunities for nutritional interventions during pregnancy, including iron-folic acid supplementation and nutrition counseling, within Indonesia's primary healthcare system (Puskesmas).

### 4.4 Child-Specific Factors and the Window of Opportunity

Low birth weight emerged as the strongest single predictor of stunting (OR = 2.97), consistent with global evidence that intrauterine growth restriction is a critical antecedent of postnatal linear growth faltering. The significant associations of suboptimal infant and young child feeding practices—non-exclusive breastfeeding (OR = 1.68) and inadequate complementary feeding (OR = 1.82)—underscore the importance of the first 1,000-day window. In Indonesia, despite high rates of ever-breastfeeding, exclusive breastfeeding rates at six months remain below 40%, and complementary feeding practices often lack dietary diversity. Recurrent infections, particularly diarrhea, amplify the risk (OR = 1.94) by impairing nutrient absorption and increasing metabolic demands, creating a vicious cycle of infection and malnutrition.

### 4.5 Socioeconomic and Environmental Pathways

The association between low household income and stunting (OR = 2.14) operates through multiple pathways, including reduced purchasing power for nutritious foods, limited access to healthcare, and residence in environments with inadequate water and sanitation infrastructure. The rural-urban disparity (OR = 1.48) reflects geographic inequities in health service delivery, infrastructure development, and economic opportunities that persist across the Indonesian archipelago. The role of inadequate sanitation (OR = 1.71) and unimproved water sources (OR = 1.43) is particularly relevant in the Indonesian context, where environmental enteric dysfunction—a subclinical condition caused by chronic exposure to fecal pathogens—may contribute to growth faltering even in the absence of clinical diarrhea. Household food insecurity (OR = 1.89) is an emerging concern, as Indonesia faces concurrent challenges of undernutrition and rising food prices.

### 4.6 Policy and Programmatic Implications

The findings of this review have several implications for stunting reduction efforts in Indonesia. First, the significant regional disparities suggest that a geographically targeted approach is necessary, with intensified interventions in high-burden provinces such as East Nusa Tenggara, Papua, and West Sulawesi. Second, the multifactorial nature of stunting determinants supports the continued implementation of integrated, multisectoral strategies under the National Strategy to Accelerate Stunting Prevention (Stranas Stunting), which coordinates interventions across health, water and sanitation, social protection, and food security sectors. Third, the strong associations with maternal nutritional status and antenatal care quality indicate that interventions must begin before conception and continue through pregnancy, rather than focusing solely on children after birth. Fourth, the modest but consistent sex difference in stunting risk (OR for male = 1.21) warrants further investigation into sex-specific growth patterns and caregiving behaviors in the Indonesian context.

### 4.7 Comparison with Regional and Global Evidence

The pooled prevalence of 31.8% places Indonesia among the countries with the highest stunting burden in Southeast Asia, comparable to Timor-Leste and Laos but higher than Vietnam (23.8%) and Thailand (10.5%). The determinants identified in this review are broadly consistent with findings from systematic reviews in other low- and middle-income countries. However, the magnitude of the association for maternal short stature is notably higher in the Indonesian context, possibly reflecting the long-term effects of historical undernutrition. The role of environmental determinants (WASH) is also more pronounced than in some other settings, consistent with Indonesia's ongoing challenges in achieving universal access to improved sanitation.

### 4.8 Strengths and Limitations

This review has several strengths. It represents the most comprehensive synthesis of stunting determinants in Indonesia to date, with a large pooled sample size, rigorous methodology following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, and a systematic assessment of publication bias. The inclusion of studies from all major Indonesian islands enhances the geographic representativeness of the findings. However, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the predominance of cross-sectional studies limits causal inference, and the temporal relationship between some determinants and stunting cannot be established definitively. Second, substantial heterogeneity was observed for most pooled estimates, which was only partially explained by meta-regression. Third, publication bias was detected for the primary outcome and some determinant analyses, suggesting that smaller studies with null findings may be underrepresented. Fourth, the exclusion of non-English and non-Indonesian language publications may have introduced language bias, although this is unlikely to substantially affect findings given the geographic scope. Fifth, variations in stunting measurement protocols and anthropometric standards across studies may contribute to measurement error.
